raw:
{
  "need": "Identity",
  "secondary": { "name": "Competence", "description": "The shutdown also masks a fear of not being capable enough to figure out what comes next — avoidance is easier than risking the wrong answer." },
  "read": "At 18, being asked about college and life plans feels like being asked to hand over a finished version of yourself before you even know who that is. Every conversation about it implicitly says 'you should already know,' which hits their status hard — like they're failing a test they never got to study for. Shutting down is a way to protect themselves from feeling exposed and behind.",
  "pull": { "collapse": "Enforcer", "instinct": "Push harder, bring up the deadlines, remind them time is running out — which just confirms to them that you see a problem with who they are right now, and they go further underground." },
  "mentorMove": "Come in without an agenda to fix, and make it clear you're curious about them as a person, not anxious about a timeline. You hold the expectation that they will think seriously about their future, but you open the floor by treating that thinking as something you do together, not something they owe you a finished answer on.",
  "holdFirm": [
    "They need to be actively engaging with questions about next steps — shutting down entirely is not an option you accept long-term.",
    "You expect real effort toward figuring this out, even if the answer is still forming."
  ],
  "stayFlexible": [
    "The conversation does not have to be about college specifically — trade programs, gap years, work, or 'I genuinely don't know yet' are all legitimate starting points.",
    "You can let them drive the format: a car ride, a walk, a meal — wherever they feel least cornered.",
    "The timeline for having a full plan is flexible; the expectation to keep thinking is not."
  ],
  "forceLevel": { "level": 2, "label": "Questions" },
  "script": [
    { "phase": "Connection", "words": "Hey, I want to talk about something, but I want to say upfront — I'm not coming in here to pressure you or push a specific answer. I know I've probably made these conversations feel like an interrogation, and that's on me." },
    { "phase": "Curiosity", "words": "When this stuff comes up and you go quiet, what's actually happening for you? Like, is it that you don't know yet, or is it that the whole thing feels overwhelming, or is it something else entirely? I genuinely want to understand what it feels like from where you're sitting." },
    { "phase": "Collaboration", "words": "Because here's what I think is true: not having it figured out at 18 does not mean something is wrong with you. Your brain is literally in the middle of building the machinery that does long-term planning — that's real, not an excuse. But I do think we need to start poking at this together, even if all we're doing at first is naming what you're curious about or what you can't stand the thought of doing with your life." },
    { "phase": "Commitment", "words": "I'm not going to drop this, because I have high standards for you and I know you're more than capable of working through hard, uncertain things. But I'm also not going to make this a thing where you feel like you have to defend yourself every time. So let's agree: we carve out some real time to think out loud together, no judgment, no 'you should already know this.' Can you give me that?" }
  ],
  "longGame": "The goal over the next several months is to shift these conversations from something they brace for into something they actually bring to you — which only happens if they learn that your presence in this is curiosity, not panic. Keep the standard visible and keep yourself calm, and eventually they'll start to see figuring out their future as something they're capable of, not a performance they might fail."
}
situation: My almost-18-year-old shuts down every time college or life after graduation comes up.
